exam_guide_revision: Reviewed anti-boring v4, 2026-09-26. Full learning and question editorial audit completed; weak/generic prompts and distractors were rewritten while preserving compatibility.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

glossary.definition: The simplest clearly correct solution used as a reference point for optimization.
The repeated expensive operation that dominates avoidable work.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

modules.title: Stop guessing patterns: make the problem show you the shape

nodes.title: The words FIRST, INDEX, and CONTIGUOUS can change the whole solution

reveal.text: A webhook processor must return the index of the FIRST repeated event ID. You are learning to extract the few prompt details that actually control the algorithm before touching code.

spans.text: A webhook processor must return the index of the FIRST repeated event ID.
You are learning to extract the few prompt details that actually control the algorithm before touching code

reveal.text: If you immediately convert the IDs to a set, duplicate membership survives but the first duplicate position disappears. That is a correct data structure solving the wrong contract.

spans.text: the transformation destroyed information the output still needs

reveal.text: Write the contract in one sentence: preserve arrival order, return an index, and detect whether the current ID appeared earlier. Now the useful state becomes obvious.

spans.text: preserve only the information the output still needs

reveal.text: Problem-shape extraction. Trigger: words such as first, index, contiguous, original order, distinct indices, sorted, or in-place change what transformations are legal

spans.text: Problem-shape extraction
words such as first, index, contiguous, original order, distinct indices, sorted, or in-place change what transformations are legal

reveal.text: A 'longest contiguous request burst' problem also cannot be reduced to an unordered bag of values. The story changed; position semantics still control the solution.

spans.text: output semantics decide which information may be discarded

reveal.text: A prompt asks for the ORIGINAL indices of two records. Is sorting values alone safe? Answer: No — not unless original indices travel with the values.

spans.text: No — not unless original indices travel with the values.

glossary.definition: The exact behavior and constraints your algorithm must preserve.

nodes.title: Make the slow solution expose its own bottleneck

reveal.text: You need to find whether any two request sizes add exactly to a capacity. You are learning to use a simple correct baseline as an X-ray for the repeated work.

spans.text: You need to find whether any two request sizes add exactly to a capacity.
You are learning to use a simple correct baseline as an X-ray for the repeated work

annotations.title: Easy to trust
annotations.explanation: Every legal pair i<j is checked exactly once.

annotations.title: The bottleneck is visible
annotations.explanation: For each i, later values are searched again and again.

reveal.text: Do not apologize for O(n²). Say what it buys you: obvious correctness. Then ask which question the inner loop answers repeatedly.

spans.text: the exact repeated question, not a guessed pattern name

reveal.text: Correct baseline → bottleneck. Trigger: when the optimized solution is not obvious, first make the repeated work concrete

spans.text: Correct baseline → bottleneck
when the optimized solution is not obvious, first make the repeated work concrete

reveal.text: Duplicate detection can start the same way: compare each ID with later IDs, then notice that 'have I seen this?' is the repeated question.

spans.text: the baseline reveals the query your future state should answer

reveal.text: In the pair-sum baseline, what repeated question is the inner search answering for current x? Answer: Whether target - x exists among the other candidate values.

spans.text: Whether target - x exists among the other candidate values.

nodes.title: Patterns are just remembered answers to repeated questions

reveal.text: The pair-sum baseline keeps searching for target - x. A range dashboard keeps re-adding the same values. You are learning to derive a pattern from the information that would eliminate repeated work.

spans.text: The pair-sum baseline keeps searching for target - x. A range dashboard keeps re-adding the same values.
You are learning to derive a pattern from the information that would eliminate repeated work

reveal.text: Memorizing 'Two Sum = hash map' works only until the surface story changes. The useful reasoning is to identify what the baseline repeatedly asks.

spans.text: keyword memorization does not transfer to unfamiliar stories

reveal.text: Ask what answer you wish you already had. For pair sum: prior values/indices. For repeated range totals: cumulative boundaries. For a rolling fixed window: the previous window state.

spans.text: remember the answer to the expensive repeated query

reveal.text: Repeated-work elimination. Trigger: the same expensive question is recomputed for overlapping or sequential states

spans.text: Repeated-work elimination
the same expensive question is recomputed for overlapping or sequential states

reveal.text: A retry deduper and a pair-sum problem look unrelated, but both can become one-pass algorithms because old information is maintained instead of rescanned.

spans.text: maintained state replaces rescanning

reveal.text: A baseline re-sums k numbers for every neighboring k-sized window. What should you remember? Answer: The previous window sum, then subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming one.

spans.text: The previous window sum, then subtract the outgoing value and add the incoming one.

nodes.title: At 100,000 items, O(n²) stops being an abstract symbol

reveal.text: A batch of 100,000 event IDs is timing out because every new ID scans all earlier IDs. You are learning to use Big O as an early scale filter instead of a math chapter.

spans.text: A batch of 100,000 event IDs is timing out because every new ID scans all earlier IDs.
You are learning to use Big O as an early scale filter instead of a math chapter

reveal.text: The code may look small, but checking roughly every pair means billions of comparisons at this scale. Micro-optimizing Python syntax will not rescue the growth shape.

spans.text: the growth rate overwhelms constant-factor tweaks

reveal.text: Estimate the shape first: direct lookup ~O(1), halving ~O(log n), one scan ~O(n), sort ~O(n log n), all pairs ~O(n²). Then decide which shapes are plausible for the input size.

spans.text: the dominant growth shape

reveal.text: Growth-rate filtering. Trigger: input constraints are large enough that the wrong asymptotic shape dominates everything else

spans.text: Growth-rate filtering
input constraints are large enough that the wrong asymptotic shape dominates everything else

reveal.text: The same filter works on a log processor, a cache warmer, or an interview array problem. The scale tells you which designs deserve attention.

spans.text: constraints eliminate implausible growth shapes before implementation details

reveal.text: At n=100,000, which deserves immediate suspicion: one scan or all-pairs comparison? Answer: All-pairs comparison — O(n²).

spans.text: All-pairs comparison — O(n²).

nodes.title: A loop inside a loop can still be linear

reveal.text: A window algorithm moves `right` forward once per item and moves `left` forward only when the window is invalid. You are learning to count total state changes across the run instead of multiplying indentation levels.

spans.text: A window algorithm moves `right` forward once per item and moves `left` forward only when the window is invalid.
You are learning to count total state changes across the run instead of multiplying indentation levels

prompts.label: THIS NESTED LOOP IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY O(n²)

annotations.title: right moves n times
annotations.explanation: It advances once through the sequence.

annotations.title: left also moves at most n times total
annotations.explanation: It never resets or moves backward.

reveal.text: Count events globally. If each element can enter and leave the maintained state once, the total work can stay linear even with a nested while.

spans.text: the total number of pointer moves / pushes / pops across the whole execution

reveal.text: Aggregate-work reasoning. Trigger: inner work consumes progress that is not reset by the outer loop

spans.text: Aggregate-work reasoning
inner work consumes progress that is not reset by the outer loop

reveal.text: Merging two sorted log feeds also uses a loop within a loop-like control flow, yet each cursor advances at most to the end once.

spans.text: monotonic cursors make total movement bounded

reveal.text: If left never moves backward, how many times can `left += 1` run over an n-item input? Answer: At most n times total.

spans.text: At most n times total.

nodes.title: Sometimes the right optimization is simply: remember what you already learned

reveal.text: A duplicate detector rescans the processed prefix for every new request ID. You are learning to recognize a time-space trade when a small amount of memory removes much larger repeated work.

spans.text: A duplicate detector rescans the processed prefix for every new request ID.
You are learning to recognize a time-space trade when a small amount of memory removes much larger repeated work

reveal.text: Using no extra memory sounds attractive, but repeated prefix scans make the runtime quadratic.

spans.text: saving memory forces the same membership question to be recomputed

reveal.text: Store seen IDs. You spend O(n) extra space to make each membership question expected O(1), turning the full scan into expected O(n).

spans.text: processed-history lookup state

reveal.text: Time-space trade-off. Trigger: the baseline repeatedly recomputes information that is cheap to store and reuse

spans.text: Time-space trade-off
the baseline repeatedly recomputes information that is cheap to store and reuse

reveal.text: Caches, memoization, prefix arrays, maps, and visited sets are all versions of the same move: pay memory to avoid repeating work.

spans.text: stored state substitutes for recomputation

reveal.text: If a set turns O(n²) duplicate checking into expected O(n), what did you buy the speed with? Answer: O(n) extra memory for the seen IDs.

spans.text: O(n) extra memory for the seen IDs.

nodes.title: Your data structure needs a sentence that says what it means right now

reveal.text: A sliding-window implementation has a frequency map, `left`, and `right`. The code works on examples but feels fragile. You are learning to state the invariant that makes maintained state trustworthy after every update.

spans.text: A sliding-window implementation has a frequency map, `left`, and `right`. The code works on examples but feels fragile.
You are learning to state the invariant that makes maintained state trustworthy after every update

reveal.text: Without a precise meaning for the map, it is easy to remove the wrong element, update counts in the wrong order, or accidentally let stale values remain.

spans.text: state exists, but nobody can say exactly what it represents

reveal.text: Write the invariant before the tricky update: 'the frequency map exactly counts elements inside the current [left, right] window.' Every add/remove must preserve that sentence.

spans.text: one precise sentence describing the maintained state

reveal.text: Loop/state invariant. Trigger: an optimization depends on mutable state that must stay synchronized with the portion of input it summarizes

spans.text: Loop/state invariant
an optimization depends on mutable state that must stay synchronized with the portion of input it summarizes

reveal.text: Binary search uses a different state but the same idea: if the target exists, it remains in the current candidate interval.

spans.text: updates are safe only if they preserve the state meaning

reveal.text: What is a useful invariant for a seen-set duplicate scan before processing index i? Answer: The set contains exactly the IDs from positions 0 through i-1.

spans.text: The set contains exactly the IDs from positions 0 through i-1.

nodes.title: A correct loop that never finishes is still broken

reveal.text: Binary search passes most tests but hangs on a two-element interval. You are learning to pair an invariant with a progress rule so the algorithm cannot repeat the same state forever.

spans.text: Binary search passes most tests but hangs on a two-element interval.
You are learning to pair an invariant with a progress rule so the algorithm cannot repeat the same state forever

annotations.title: Can make no progress
annotations.explanation: When mid == left, the next iteration can recreate the exact same interval.

annotations.title: This side removes mid
annotations.explanation: The right boundary strictly decreases here.

reveal.text: Once `mid` is proven too small, remove it: `left = mid + 1`. Now the candidate interval strictly shrinks.

spans.text: a quantity that strictly advances or shrinks every non-terminal iteration

reveal.text: Progress measure. Trigger: a loop narrows candidates, moves pointers, consumes work, or explores states

spans.text: Progress measure
a loop narrows candidates, moves pointers, consumes work, or explores states

reveal.text: A graph traversal marks discoveries so it does not cycle forever; a two-pointer scan advances at least one cursor each iteration. Different pattern, same progress requirement.

spans.text: every iteration must make the remaining problem strictly smaller

reveal.text: Why is `left = mid + 1` better than `left = mid` after proving `values[mid] < target`? Answer: It discards the proven-impossible midpoint and guarantees the interval shrinks.

spans.text: It discards the proven-impossible midpoint and guarantees the interval shrinks.

nodes.title: Do not 'test more' — attack the exact assumption you just made

reveal.text: Your two-sum code uses a hash map and looks correct. Now try to break the distinct-index logic. You are learning to choose tiny hostile tests that target boundaries, duplicates, and state-update assumptions.

spans.text: Your two-sum code uses a hash map and looks correct. Now try to break the distinct-index logic.
You are learning to choose tiny hostile tests that target boundaries, duplicates, and state-update assumptions

reveal.text: A huge random test may pass while missing the one bug where the algorithm reuses the same index or skips the last candidate.

spans.text: broad testing does not necessarily attack the reasoning risk

reveal.text: Use surgical cases: empty/one item, smallest nontrivial input, duplicates, answer at first/last position, and no answer.

spans.text: a test that directly challenges the algorithm's invariant or boundary rule

reveal.text: Counterexample-driven testing. Trigger: the algorithm relies on a boundary convention, duplicate rule, or state-update ordering

spans.text: Counterexample-driven testing
the algorithm relies on a boundary convention, duplicate rule, or state-update ordering

reveal.text: For pair sum, `[3]` target 6 must be false while `[3,3]` target 6 must be true. For binary search, test two items and absent values at both ends.

spans.text: tiny cases expose logical mistakes faster than random volume

reveal.text: Which test catches illegal self-reuse in a pair-sum algorithm with target 6? Answer: `[3]` — one value cannot supply two distinct indices.

spans.text: `[3]` — one value cannot supply two distinct indices.
